title: Narcissus. Echo
titleEn: Narcissus and Echo, 2 of 2 — Metamorphoses III.437–510
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 fb3fdb1d8a4a3b82. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Narcissus cannot be got away from the pool, and lies in the grass staring at the reflection until he dies of it. He calls out to the woods, argues with the figure in the water, and at last works out that it is himself — which frees him from nothing, since what he wants he already is. He beats his bared breast, melts like wax at a low flame, and dies still looking; Echo, who had once loved him and is angry still, gives back his last cries and his farewell. When the nymphs come with pyre and bier there is no body to burn, only a flower.

sentences.t:
Non illum Cereris, non illum cura quietis
abstrahere inde potest, sed opaca fusus in herba
spectat inexpleto mendacem lumine formam,
perque oculos perit ipse suos;
sentences.l: Neither concern for Ceres nor concern for rest can drag him away from there, but, poured out on the shaded grass, he gazes at the lying shape with an unfilled eye, and through his own eyes he himself perishes.
sentences.i: No thought of food, no thought of sleep can draw him from the place; spread out in the shaded grass he stares at the lying shape with an eye that cannot be filled, and perishes by way of his own eyes.
sentences.n: One noun, cura, governs both genitives: Ceres, the goddess of grain, stands by metonymy for food, as quies does for sleep. fusus is the participle of fundo, to pour, used of a body laid out at full length. lumine is a singular for the eyes, and inexpleto is literally "unfilled" — an eye that nothing puts an end to. The last clause turns the ordinary organ of looking into the instrument of his death.

sentences.t:
paulumque levatus
ad circumstantes tendens sua bracchia silvas
“ecquis, io silvae, crudelius” inquit “amavit?
sentences.l: and raised a little, stretching his own arms toward the woods standing round, “has anyone, oh woods, loved more cruelly?” he says.
sentences.i: And lifting himself a little, reaching his arms out to the woods that stood around him: “Has anyone ever loved more cruelly, oh you woods?” he said.
sentences.n: levatus is "having been raised", of propping himself up from the grass he is lying in. circumstantes silvas are the woods standing round the pool. ecquis opens a question that expects the answer no. crudelius is the neuter comparative adverb, "more cruelly", so what he asks about is the manner of the loving and not the cruelty of the beloved. inquit is dropped in parenthetically between the quoted words, as Latin regularly places it.

sentences.t: Scitis enim, et multis latebra opportuna fuistis.
sentences.l: For you know, and you have been a convenient hiding-place to many.
sentences.i: You know, of course: many have found a hiding place ready in you.
sentences.n: The woods are addressed as witnesses of other people's love affairs. latebra opportuna is a hiding-place that comes at the right moment, and multis is the dative of those it served. fuistis is second person plural, still speaking to the silvae he has just called on.

sentences.t:
Ecquem, cum vestrae tot agantur saecula vitae,
qui sic tabuerit, longo meministis in aevo?
sentences.l: Anyone at all — since so many generations of your life are being lived through — who has so wasted away, do you remember in your long age?
sentences.i: In all your long span, and so many generations of it have gone by, do you remember anyone who wasted away like this?
sentences.n: ecquem is the emphatic interrogative "anyone at all", and it is the accusative object of meministis. The relative clause qui sic tabuerit has the subjunctive of characteristic: anyone of the kind who has wasted away in this way. cum ... agantur is causal, "seeing that so many ages of your life are being lived through". saecula are generations or lifetimes: trees outlast men, which is the whole reason for asking them.

sentences.t:
Et placet et video; sed quod videoque placetque,
non tamen invenio: tantus tenet error amantem.
sentences.l: Both he pleases and I see [him]; but what I both see and [what] pleases, I nevertheless do not find: so great a wandering holds the lover.
sentences.i: He pleases me, and I can see him; and yet what I see and what pleases me I still cannot find — so complete a delusion holds the lover fast.
sentences.n: placet has the boy for its subject with the person pleased left unexpressed. quod videoque placetque is a single relative clause serving both verbs, its antecedent not stated: the thing seen is the thing that pleases and the thing not found, all one. error is the strong sense of the noun, a straying or a being led astray, not a mistake of fact. amantem is Narcissus speaking of himself in the third person, at the moment he is furthest from recognising himself.

sentences.t:
Quoque magis doleam, nec nos mare separat ingens,
nec via nec montes nec clausis moenia portis:
exigua prohibemur aqua.
sentences.l: And so that I may grieve the more, no huge sea separates us, nor road nor mountains nor walls with closed gates: we are kept apart by a scanty water.
sentences.i: And — to make the grief the greater — no vast sea divides us, no road, no mountains, no walls with their gates shut: a thin skin of water keeps us apart.
sentences.n: Quoque here is quo + -que, not the adverb "also": quo with a comparative introduces a purpose clause, "and so that I may grieve the more". The negatives pile up the obstacles that are not there so that the one that is looks absurd. clausis portis is an ablative of description attached to moenia — walls with their gates shut — and not an ablative absolute: the gates are a feature of the walls, not a separate circumstance. prohibemur is passive with the ablative of the thing that keeps them apart, and its plural covers Narcissus and the reflection.

sentences.t:
Cupit ipse teneri:
nam quotiens liquidis porreximus oscula lymphis,
hic totiens ad me resupino nititur ore.
sentences.l: He himself desires to be held: for as often as we have stretched kisses out to the clear waters, so often does he strain toward me with mouth bent back.
sentences.i: He wants to be held, he does: as often as I have reached my kisses down to the clear water, so often he presses up toward me with his face tilted back.
sentences.n: teneri is the passive infinitive, "to be held", so the reflection is credited with wanting exactly what Narcissus wants. porreximus is a poetic plural for the singular, "I have stretched out", and liquidis lymphis is the dative of what the kisses are offered to. nititur is deponent — passive in form, active in sense — "he strains, he presses". resupino ore is an ablative of manner: the face in the water is upside down to his own, tilted back toward him.

sentences.t: Posse putes tangi: minimum est, quod amantibus obstat.
sentences.l: You would think [him] able to be touched: it is the smallest thing that stands in the lovers' way.
sentences.i: You would think he could be touched — the thing that blocks the lovers is so small.
sentences.n: putes is a potential subjunctive addressed to no one in particular, "you would think". posse tangi is the infinitive clause depending on it, with its accusative subject left to be supplied from the context — the figure in the water, so English needs a bracketed "him". amantibus is the dative after obstat, and it is plural: he counts the two of them as lovers.

sentences.t:
Quisquis es, huc exi! quid me, puer unice, fallis,
quove petitus abis?
sentences.l: Whoever you are, come out here! why, matchless boy, do you cheat me, or to where do you go off when sought?
sentences.i: Whoever you are, come out to me! Why do you cheat me, boy beyond compare, and where do you go off to when I come after you?
sentences.n: exi is the imperative of exeo, "come out": he is asking the figure to leave the water. unice is "one of a kind, without a match". petitus is a perfect passive participle agreeing with the person addressed, "having been sought after", which English can only turn into a clause. quove is quo + -ve, "or to where", so the question asks the destination, not the reason.

sentences.t:
certe nec forma nec aetas
est mea quam fugias, et amarunt me quoque nymphae.
sentences.l: certainly neither my beauty nor my age is [such] that you should flee it, and nymphs have loved me too.
sentences.i: Surely neither my looks nor my years are anything to run from — and I have been loved too, by nymphs.
sentences.n: quam fugias is a relative clause of characteristic with the subjunctive: of a kind that you would flee. forma and aetas are both feminine and quam picks up the nearer of them, with est singular after the pair. amarunt is the syncopated form of amaverunt. quoque here is the plain adverb, and it stands after me, the word it emphasises: he too is a person who has been loved. The word that opens line 448 is the other one, quo + -que.

sentences.t:
Spem mihi nescio quam vultu promittis amico,
cumque ego porrexi tibi bracchia, porrigis ultro:
sentences.l: You promise me I know not what hope with a friendly face, and when I have stretched my arms out to you, you stretch yours out unasked.
sentences.i: With that friendly look you promise me some hope or other, and when I reach my arms toward you, you reach yours out of your own accord.
sentences.n: nescio quam is a fixed idiom that has stopped behaving like a verb — "some ... or other" — and it governs no question. porrexi and porrigis put the same verb in both mouths, the change of tense marking that his own gesture came first. ultro is not "further" but "unprompted, on one's own initiative", which is the one thing a reflection cannot be.

sentences.t:
cum risi, adrides; lacrimas quoque saepe notavi
me lacrimante tuas, nutu quoque signa remittis,
sentences.l: when I have laughed, you laugh back; often too I have noticed your tears, with me weeping, and you send back signals with a nod as well.
sentences.i: When I laugh, you laugh back; and often, while I was weeping, I have caught sight of your tears; and you return signs to me with a nod.
sentences.n: adrides is ad- + rideo, "you laugh back at me"; Magnus keeps the unassimilated adr- spelling. me lacrimante has the shape of an ablative absolute, "with me weeping", though its pronoun is the same person as the subject of notavi, so it is not absolute in the strict sense — the participle simply has no other way to attach. tuas is held back a whole line from the lacrimas it agrees with, so the tears are named before they are said to be his.

sentences.t:
et quantum motu formosi suspicor oris,
verba refers aures non pervenientia nostras.
sentences.l: and as far as I guess from the movement of your beautiful mouth, you return words not reaching our ears.
sentences.i: and, so far as I can guess from the movement of that lovely mouth, you send words back that never reach my ears.
sentences.n: quantum is an accusative of extent used adverbially, "to the degree that". motu is the ablative of what the guess is drawn from. pervenientia is a present participle agreeing with verba, and the pair aures ... nostras is split to stand on either side of non pervenientia, so that in the Latin the words are visibly stopped short of the ears. nostras is again a poetic plural for "my".

sentences.t: Iste ego sum: sensi, nec me mea fallit imago.
sentences.l: That one is I: I have felt it, and my own image does not deceive me.
sentences.i: That boy is myself. I know it now; my own reflection does not deceive me.
sentences.n: iste is the demonstrative of the second person — "that one there, the one you are looking at" — so Narcissus is still half-addressing the figure in the water at the very moment he identifies it as himself. sensi is a perfect of sudden realisation: not "I feel" but "it has come home to me."

sentences.t: Uror amore mei, flammas moveoque feroque.
sentences.l: I am burned with love of myself, and I both stir the flames and bear them.
sentences.i: I burn with love of my own self; I light the fire and I suffer it.
sentences.n: Uror is passive, "I am set alight" — the ordinary Latin way of saying a person is in love, and here the passive is exact, since he is what is burning. mei is the genitive of ego and it is objective: love directed at me, not love belonging to me. The doubled -que ... -que sets the one who kindles against the one who endures, and he is both.

sentences.t:
Quid faciam? roger, anne rogem? quid deinde rogabo?
quod cupio mecum est: inopem me copia fecit.
sentences.l: What am I to do? Am I to be asked, or am I to ask? What shall I ask for then? What I desire is with me: abundance has made me destitute.
sentences.i: What am I to do? Be courted, or court? And what would I ask for then? What I want is here with me: having everything has left me with nothing.
sentences.n: faciam, roger and rogem are deliberative subjunctives — questions about what is to be done, not about what is the case — and rogabo that follows is a plain future, so the sequence slides from "what am I to ask" to "what will I actually ask". roger is passive: am I to be the one who is asked. anne is the fuller form of an, introducing the second half of the alternative. The last clause is built on two flat opposites, inops and copia: what he has is precisely what he lacks.

sentences.t:
O utinam a nostro secedere corpore possem!
Votum in amante novum: vellem quod amamus abesset! —
sentences.l: O if only I could withdraw from our own body! A wish new in a lover: I would wish that what we love were absent!
sentences.i: Oh, if only I could get away from my own body! A strange thing for a lover to want: I wish that what I love were gone!
sentences.n: utinam with the imperfect subjunctive possem is the wish for what is not so and cannot be. nostro corpore is a poetic plural for "my body", as amamus is for "I love". vellem is likewise a past subjunctive of unreal wish, and abesset follows it with no conjunction between, which is how volo and its relatives take a subjunctive clause. Magnus prints a dash at the end of this line; the speech runs on, but the editor marks the pause where the complaint turns into a death-speech.

sentences.t:
Iamque dolor vires adimit, nec tempora vitae
longa meae superant, primoque exstinguor in aevo.
sentences.l: And already grief takes my strength away, nor do the long spans of my life remain, and I am put out in my first age.
sentences.i: Already the pain is taking my strength; no long stretch of life is left me; I am snuffed out in my earliest years.
sentences.n: tempora vitae longa meae is pulled apart across the line end — the noun, then its genitive, then the adjective belonging to the noun and the possessive belonging to the genitive — and English can do no more than put the pieces back in order. exstinguor is passive, "I am put out", keeping the fire he called down on himself at line 464. Magnus prints the exst- spelling the edition uses throughout. primo in aevo is the first stretch of a life.

sentences.t:
Nec mihi mors gravis est posituro morte dolores:
hic, qui diligitur, vellem diuturnior esset.
sentences.l: Nor is death heavy for me, about to lay down my griefs by death: this one, who is loved, I could wish were longer-lasting.
sentences.i: Death is no hard thing for me, since by dying I shall set my griefs down; but I could wish that he, the one who is loved, might last longer.
sentences.n: posituro is a future participle in the dative agreeing with mihi, "for me, who am going to lay aside". morte is the ablative of means, so death is at once what he does not fear and the instrument that puts the pain down. diligitur is passive, "is loved", and leaves the lover unnamed, which is the whole joke: the lover is the speaker. vellem stands with esset and nothing between them, exactly as vellem stands with abesset at line 468.

sentences.t: Nunc duo concordes anima moriemur in una.”
sentences.l: Now we two, agreeing, shall die in one soul.
sentences.i: Now we two, at one with each other, will die in a single life.
sentences.n: concordes is "of one heart", the word used of lovers who are in accord, and the irony is that there is only one heart present. anima is breath, then life, then soul; in una anima is the single life the two of them must share because they are one person. Elsewhere in the speech the plural is poetic and means "I"; here duo makes it real.

sentences.t:
Dixit et ad faciem rediit male sanus eandem
et lacrimis turbavit aquas, obscuraque moto
reddita forma lacu est.
sentences.l: He spoke, and, badly sound in mind, went back to the same face, and troubled the waters with tears, and the shape was given back darkened, the pool having been stirred.
sentences.i: He had done speaking, and, out of his senses, turned back to the same face and stirred the water with his tears; the pool moved, and the image came back darkened.
sentences.n: male sanus is "badly sound", the Latin way of saying a man is not in his right mind: male negates the adjective rather than qualifying it. moto lacu is a true ablative absolute — the pool is neither subject nor object of the main clause, whose subject is forma. obscura is predicative with reddita: the shape does not merely come back, it comes back dark. What ruins the sight is the weeping he does over it.

sentences.t:
Quam cum vidisset abire,
“quo refugis? remane, nec me, crudelis, amantem
desere!” clamavit: “liceat, quod tangere non est,
adspicere et misero praebere alimenta furori.”
sentences.l: And when he had seen her going away, “where are you fleeing back to? stay, and do not, cruel one, desert me who love you!” he cried: “let it be permitted to look at what it is not possible to touch, and to furnish food to a wretched madness.”
sentences.i: And when he saw her going, “Where are you going? Stay — don't leave me, cruel as you are, when I love you!” he cried. “Let me at least look at what I cannot touch, and give my wretched madness what it feeds on.”
sentences.n: Quam is a connecting relative picking up forma from the line before — "and when he had seen her going away" — and the feminine is the grammatical gender of the shape, not a person's. quo is "to where", so the question is where he is escaping to, not why he is escaping. quod tangere non est keeps the old impersonal non est for "it is not possible". alimenta furori praebere is a feeding metaphor — the madness is fed, and the poem's language of being consumed picks it up.

sentences.t:
Dumque dolet, summa vestem deduxit ab ora
nudaque marmoreis percussit pectora palmis.
sentences.l: And while he grieves, he drew the garment down from its topmost edge and struck his bared breast with marble palms.
sentences.i: And in his grief he pulled his robe down from the neck of it and beat his bared breast with hands like marble.
sentences.n: dum keeps the present indicative dolet beside the perfect deduxit, which is its regular habit whatever the tense of the main verb. summa ab ora is "from the topmost edge" — the neck of the garment, dragged down to bare the chest. marmoreis carries the colour and the hardness at once, the white of statuary; that same whiteness returns two lines later in the apple that is pale on one side.

sentences.t:
Pectora traxerunt tenuem percussa ruborem,
non aliter quam poma solent, quae candida parte,
parte rubent,
sentences.l: The struck breast drew on a faint redness, not otherwise than apples are accustomed to do, which are white in the one part, in the other part redden,
sentences.i: The beaten breast took on a faint flush, just as apples do that are pale on one side and reddening on the other,
sentences.n: percussa is a perfect passive participle agreeing with pectora: the blow is already over and the colour is what follows it. traxerunt is "drew on", of taking a colour into oneself. non aliter quam is the standard formula opening a simile, "not otherwise than". quae candida parte, parte rubent balances one ablative of respect against the other with no connective between them. Magnus prints tenuem, a thin or faint redness; some editions print roseum, which names the colour rose instead of measuring how little of it there is.

sentences.t:
aut ut variis solet uva racemis
ducere purpureum nondum matura colorem.
sentences.l: or as a grape in its dappled clusters is accustomed, not yet ripe, to draw on a purple colour.
sentences.i: or as the grape in its mottled bunches draws on its purple before it is ripe.
sentences.n: uva is the bunch of grapes, racemis the stalks it hangs in, and variis says the bunch is not one colour yet: some berries have turned and some have not. nondum matura agrees with uva and is concessive in force — the colour arrives before the ripeness does. ducere colorem is the same idiom as traxerunt ruborem at line 482, a thing drawing a colour onto itself, and that is what ties both similes back to the blush.

sentences.t:
Quae simul adspexit liquefacta rursus in unda,
non tulit ulterius,
sentences.l: And when he caught sight of these things in the water made liquid again, he bore it no further,
sentences.i: And the moment he caught sight of all this in the water, gone clear again, he could bear no more,
sentences.n: Quae is a connecting relative, neuter plural, gathering up the blush of the lines before: "and these things". simul is short for simul ac, "as soon as". liquefacta agrees with unda — the water that has settled and run clear again now that his tears have stopped disturbing it. The same root comes back four lines on in liquitur, where the one who melts is he.

sentences.t:
sed ut intabescere flavae
igne levi cerae matutinaeque pruinae
sole tepente solent, sic attenuatus amore
liquitur et tecto paulatim carpitur igni.
sentences.l: but as yellow waxes are accustomed to melt away at a light fire, and morning frosts with the sun growing warm, so, thinned out by love, he melts and is little by little plucked away by a covered fire.
sentences.i: but as yellow wax melts at a low flame, and morning frost melts as the sun grows warm, so, worn thin by love, he dissolves, and a hidden fire eats him away little by little.
sentences.n: One verb carries two subjects: flavae cerae and matutinae pruinae are both nominative plurals with solent, and intabescere is the infinitive depending on it. sole tepente is an ablative absolute, "with the sun growing warm". attenuatus is "thinned", from a verb for drawing something out fine. tecto igni is a fire under cover, the ablative of what wears him away, and carpitur is "is plucked at", of a thing taken a little at a time — which paulatim then says outright.

sentences.t:
Et neque iam color est mixto candore rubori,
nec vigor et vires et quae modo visa placebant,
nec corpus remanet, quondam quod amaverat Echo.
sentences.l: And now there is no colour, with the whiteness mingled into the red, nor vigour and strength and the things which, seen just now, were pleasing, nor does the body remain which Echo had once loved.
sentences.i: And now the colour is gone, the white blended into the red; gone the vigour and the strength and everything that a moment ago was a pleasure to look at; and the body is gone that Echo once loved.
sentences.n: mixto candore rubori is an ablative of description attached to color, "colour with its white mingled into its red", with rubori the dative that misceo takes; it can equally be read as an ablative absolute, and the English is the same either way. In quae modo visa placebant, visa is a perfect passive participle agreeing with quae — the things which, once seen, went on pleasing — and the imperfect placebant makes the pleasure repeated. Three negatives strip away first the colour, then vigour and beauty together, then the body itself. amaverat is pluperfect: Echo's love was over before this scene began, and her name is the last word of the paragraph.

sentences.t:
Quae tamen ut vidit, quamvis irata memorque,
indoluit,
sentences.l: And yet when she saw these things, though angry and remembering, she felt pain at it,
sentences.i: But when she saw it, angry as she was and with nothing forgotten, she grieved for him,
sentences.n: Quae is again a connecting relative, neuter plural, the object of vidit — "and these things" — while the subject of the sentence is Echo, named at the end of the line before. quamvis irata memorque concedes both at once, that she is angry and that she has not forgotten; line 493 has just said that she had once loved him. ut with the perfect indicative vidit is temporal, "when". indoluit is in- + doleo, the pain felt at something.

sentences.t:
quotiensque puer miserabilis “eheu”
dixerat, haec resonis iterabat vocibus “eheu”;
sentences.l: and as often as the pitiable boy had said “alas”, she kept repeating “alas” with resounding voices.
sentences.i: and every time the poor boy had said “Alas”, she gave back “Alas” in her echoing voice.
sentences.n: quotiens with the pluperfect dixerat and the imperfect iterabat is the construction of repeated action: whenever he had said it, she was saying it again. resonis vocibus is an ablative of manner, plural because the sound comes back more than once. Both mouths take the identical English word, and the identity is the point: she has nothing of her own to say, and what she returns is exactly and only what he gave her.

sentences.t:
cumque suos manibus percusserat ille lacertos,
haec quoque reddebat sonitum plangoris eundem.
sentences.l: and whenever he had struck his own arms with his hands, she too gave back the same sound of beating.
sentences.i: and whenever he had beaten his arms with his hands, she too gave back that same sound of mourning.
sentences.n: cum with the pluperfect indicative percusserat is iterative, "whenever", the same construction as the quotiens just above. ille and haec stand against each other, he and she, in successive lines. plangor is the noun of formal mourning, the blow and the noise of the blow at once. reddebat is "was giving back", the verb of a returned sound: what reaches him is his own noise, so that even her grief is not her own.

sentences.t:
Ultima vox solitam fuit haec spectantis in undam,
“heu frustra dilecte puer!” totidemque remisit
verba locus, dictoque vale “vale!” inquit et Echo.
sentences.l: this was the last utterance of him gazing into the accustomed water: “alas, boy loved in vain!” and the place sent back as many words, and, farewell having been said, “farewell!” said Echo too.
sentences.i: These were his last words as he gazed into the pool he knew: “Alas, boy loved in vain!” The place sent back as many words; and when he had said farewell, Echo said “Farewell” too.
sentences.n: spectantis is a genitive present participle with no noun expressed, "of him gazing", and solitam ... in undam is the water he is used to. dicto vale is an ablative absolute built on the indeclinable vale pressed into service as a noun — "farewell having been said." The scene ends as it began, with Echo unable to say anything of her own; this time the repetition lands as grief rather than as a joke.

sentences.t:
Ille caput viridi fessum submisit in herba;
lumina mors clausit domini mirantia formam.
sentences.l: He let his weary head sink down in the green grass; death closed the eyes of their master, eyes marvelling at the shape.
sentences.i: He let his tired head sink into the green grass, and death closed the eyes of the man they served, still marvelling at the shape.
sentences.n: caput viridi fessum ... in herba sets the adjective for the grass against the adjective for the head and keeps both nouns away from them, so that in the Latin the green and the weariness touch. in herba is in with the ablative after a verb of putting down, so the head comes to rest in the grass rather than being driven into it. domini is a genitive with lumina, "their master's eyes", speaking of the eyes almost as servants of the man. mirantia is a present participle agreeing with lumina: they are still marvelling at the instant they are shut. The shape they marvel at is the one in the water, which is his own.

sentences.t:
Tunc quoque se, postquam est inferna sede receptus,
in Stygia spectabat aqua.
sentences.l: Then too, after he was received into the seat below, he kept gazing at himself in the Stygian water.
sentences.i: Even then, once he had been taken into his place below, he went on gazing at himself in the water of the Styx.
sentences.n: quoque here is the plain adverb, "even then". postquam takes the perfect indicative, est ... receptus, with the auxiliary est separated from its participle receptus by inferna sede. inferna sede is an ablative of place with no preposition, as verse allows. spectabat is imperfect, and the tense is the point: the gazing has no end even after death. Styx is the river of the dead, and Stygia aqua means simply the water down there.

sentences.t:
Planxere sorores
naides et sectos fratri posuere capillos,
planxerunt dryades: plangentibus adsonat Echo.
sentences.l: His sisters the naiads beat their breasts and laid shorn hair down for their brother, the dryads beat their breasts: to those beating, Echo sounds in answer.
sentences.i: His sisters the naiads beat their breasts and laid their cut hair for their brother; the dryads beat their breasts; and to their beating Echo sounds an answer.
sentences.n: Planxere and posuere are the poetic third-person plural perfect in -ere for -erunt, and the very next line prints the full planxerunt, so both forms stand within a line of each other. plango is the verb of formal mourning, the striking of the breast, and it needs no object. sectos ... capillos posuere is the funeral offering of cut hair laid down for the dead. The naiads are water-nymphs, and the poem calls them his sisters. adsonat is a historic present and takes the dative plangentibus: she sounds in answer to those who beat — still giving back only what she is given.

sentences.t:
Iamque rogum quassasque faces feretrumque parabant:
nusquam corpus erat;
sentences.l: And now they were preparing the pyre and the shaken torches and the bier: nowhere was the body.
sentences.i: And by now they were making ready the pyre, the brandished torches, the bier — and the body was nowhere.
sentences.n: quassas is the perfect participle of quatio, "shaken": funeral torches were swung through the air to make them catch and flare. rogus is the pyre, feretrum the bier a body is carried on, and the enclitic -que heaps the three preparations together so that the short clause after the colon lands the harder. parabant is imperfect, the work still going on at the moment it turns out to be pointless; the subject is the nymphs of the lines before.

sentences.t:
croceum pro corpore florem
inveniunt, foliis medium cingentibus albis.
sentences.l: in place of the body they find a saffron flower, with white leaves encircling the middle.
sentences.i: In place of a body they find a flower with a saffron heart, ringed about with white petals.
sentences.n: inveniunt is a historic present following the imperfect parabant, and the switch of tense is what makes the discovery abrupt. croceum is saffron-yellow. foliis medium cingentibus albis is a genuine ablative absolute — its noun is neither subject nor object of inveniunt — with medium, "the middle part", as the object of the participle, and albis held to the end of the line away from the foliis it agrees with. The flower described, a yellow centre inside a ring of white, is the narcissus, which carries the boy's name.
